records.mirror_caption:
The Royal Navy during the Second World War  
Mulberry Harbour: One of the concrete caissons (Phoenixes) being towed by a tug to its assembly point to form part of a Mulberry Harbour. On reaching the Normandy shore, sea cocks on each section were opened and the huge caissons settled on the harbour bed.
records.creator: Allen, E E (Lt), Royal Navy official photographer
records.disposition: Phoenix caisson under tow; candidate for tow/caisson section.

An Invasion Rehearsal Off the Isle of Wight, 24 -28 April 1944  
A tug tows a Bombardon (part of Mulberry harbour).
records.creator: Allen, E E (Lt), Royal Navy official photographer

records.mirror_caption:
A concrete caisson or 'Phoenix', part of the Mulberry artificial harbour for D-Day, under construction, 27 January 1944.  
Construction in Britain: An early stage in the construction of a large concrete caisson, known as a Phoenix. The Phoenix units were fitted with flooding valves to allow sinking on site to form a breakwater.
records.creator: War Office official photographer, Morris (Sgt)
records.disposition: Phoenix under construction; candidate for construction section.

records.mirror_caption: 26-G-2963: Normandy Invasion, June 1944.  Violent Storm Battered Normandy Breakwater of Sunken Freighters during Invasion Landings.  Reducing the violence of a storm that blew in upon Normandy invasion operations soon after D-Day, a breakwater of sunken freighters shielded Allied landings and cut down the toll of destruction.  Coast Guard officers, thoroughly briefed in their job, helped direct the planned sinking of 23 ships to form a breakwater.   Photographed from a Coast Guard LCI (L) shows a mountainous wave spending its fury against the bulwark, June 1944.  (5/19/2015).
records.creator: National Museum of the U.S. Navy
records.disposition: Wave breaking against a sunken-ship breakwater; not wrecked Phoenix caissons or storm aftermath.
